newsitem.title: BERMUDA: Commonwealth ponders merits of capital flows.
newsitem.headline: Commonwealth ponders merits of capital flows.

text.p: Commonwealth finance ministers, who represent a quarter of the world's population, on Wednesday tried to decide whether the wave of capital invested in developing economies was a blessing or a curse.
In the 1970s, the private sector invested about $1 billion a year into the developing world.

That figure is now about $170 billion and, after the near collapse of the Mexican economy two years ago as investors pulled out their money there, other poorer countries wonder if it will be their turn next.
"I agree we need to liberalise more. But though desirable, private capital can have a negative impact," Kenyan finance minister Musalia Mudavadi told Reuters.
Most of the 53 members of a group that once comprised the British Empire are developing nations, many of them saddled with huge debts and little hope of attracting large sums from private investors.
One Commonwealth source said it was crucial to find some way to tempt funds into countries that had so far failed to attract investors.
"There is no single right way to handle capital surges," he said.

Some countries argued that capital controls were useful as long as they were for the short-term, while others said the key was for a country to make sure that its economy was being managed properly rather than try to hide behind protectionism.
"To reap the full potential from international capital flows all countries must press on with liberalisation," British Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke said.
While he conceded that some governments were wary of a rush of money, it would be a mistake not to open up their economies.
Canada's finance minister Paul Martin said there was consensus that if a country were to impose controls they should only be short term.
"There was overwhelming agreement that no restrictions would substitute for sound economic policy," he told Reuters.
He had the support of Botswana's finance minister, F.G. Mogae.
"(Developing countries) should continue to pursue policies of liberalisation," Mogae said.
